planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; give it a permanent, undisturbed spot since it clumps slowly rather than running.

directions: Native to montane forests of Yunnan Province, China, this rhizomatous mayapple typically produces a pair of rounded, toothed, leathery leaves on branching stems rather than the single leaf typical of many mayapples, giving established clumps a fuller, layered look. Nodding, pear-shaped maroon-purple flowers dangle from the junction between the paired leaf stalks in late spring, mostly hidden beneath the foliage canopy. Compared with the taller Chinese mayapple already in this dataset, mairei stays lower and more compact, making it a good scale match for smaller shaded borders. Provide the same rich, humus-heavy, evenly moist soil favored by other Asian mayapples and divide dormant rhizomes in fall to increase stock.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; mulch the crown over winter at the colder end of its range.

directions: Collected from shaded forest understories in Yunnan, this rare Chinese mayapple is named for its distinctive orange-red leaf and flower stalks, a color unmatched by any other Podophyllum already in this dataset. Its broad, glossy, umbrella-shaped leaves are held atop these colorful stems, with pale creamy-white flowers opening beneath the foliage before giving way to fruit later in the season. It remains scarce in cultivation and is often crossed with Podophyllum hexandrum by breeders seeking to combine the orange stem color with hardier growth. Give it the same cool, evenly moist, shaded woodland conditions preferred by its Asian relatives.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil beside a shaded stream, pond edge, or bog garden; keep the crown from ever drying out.

directions: Native to wet, shaded forest margins and streambanks across Japan, this royal fern relative produces upright, arching fronds with a subtle blue-green cast that sets it apart from the purely green foliage of Osmunda japonica and Osmunda regalis already in this dataset. Its fertile fronds carry rusty-brown spore clusters at the tips atop wiry, dark mahogany-colored stems. Where its range overlaps with Osmunda japonica in the wild, the two species readily hybridize into the naturally occurring cross Osmunda x intermedia. Keep the crown consistently moist in a humus-rich shaded bed or bog edge, since like other Osmunda it struggles wherever the soil is allowed to dry out.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give it room since it forms a non-spreading clump roughly two feet across.

directions: Native to moist mountain woodlands of China, Japan, and Korea, this semi-evergreen fern is easily recognized by its winged fronds, in which the lowest pair of pinnae grow dramatically longer than the rest, giving each frond a distinctive three-pronged, arrow-like silhouette unlike any other Polystichum already in this dataset. Fronds emerge glossy dark green and hold an upright, slightly arching posture through the growing season. It forms a tidy, non-spreading clump and combines well with other woodland shade perennials as a textural accent. Provide steady moisture and rich, well-drained soil, since it is less drought-tolerant once established than many of its Polystichum relatives.

planting.note: Tuck divisions into lean, sharply drained rocky or gritty soil in a shaded to partly shaded rock garden or scree bed; avoid rich, moisture-retentive woodland soil, which does not mimic its native serpentine habitat.

directions: Restricted in the wild to serpentine rock outcrops and mineral-poor ultramafic soils in the mountains of California, Oregon, Washington, and British Columbia, this small evergreen fern forms tight tufts of narrow fronds whose overlapping, folded leaflets give the whole leaf a nearly cylindrical, twisted look distinct from the flatter fronds of other native Polystichum in this dataset. It stays low and slow-growing, rarely exceeding about a foot in height even at maturity. Because it is adapted to lean, rocky soils, it performs best in sharply drained scree or rock-garden plantings rather than rich, moist woodland beds. Give it the same cool root zone and light shade favored by kruckebergii and other western rock ferns already in this dataset.
sources: Idaho Fish and Game Species Database

planting.note: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in bright shade; it establishes slowly, so avoid disturbing young plants for the first couple of seasons.

directions: Native to woodlands of China, Japan, and Korea, this compact evergreen fern produces stiff, leathery, twice-divided fronds with sharply toothed leaflets arranged in a broader, more triangular outline than the closely related tsus-simense already in this dataset. Its slightly rough-textured, emerald-green foliage forms a neat, low shuttlecock rarely reaching much beyond a foot tall. It is slow to establish but proves reliably hardy once settled, tolerating more cold than its compact size might suggest. Grow it as a small-scale companion to larger woodland ferns rather than as a standalone specimen.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Site divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in a sheltered, shaded gully-like setting; let bulbil plantlets that root along larger fronds remain in place if a naturalized colony is wanted.

directions: Native to cool, moist gullies and forest margins of southeastern Australia and Tasmania, this robust evergreen fern earns its common name from the small plantlets, or bulbils, that form near the tips of its larger fronds and root themselves in the soil below to start new plants, a habit not shared by any other Polystichum already in this dataset. Its arching, dark-green fronds carry rows of sori tucked beneath large, umbrella-shaped covers along the underside. It forms a substantial, fountain-like clump considerably larger than most other holly ferns here. Keep the soil consistently moist in a sheltered, humus-rich shaded setting reminiscent of its native forest gullies.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online (POWO)
